analysis.one_liner: Charges fossil fuel producers a rising carbon fee and rebates most of the money as monthly dividends.
analysis.headline: A carbon fee-and-dividend bill from two Democratic senators never got a committee vote; it sat in the Senate Finance Committee from July 2019 until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tax oil, gas, coal, and fluorinated gas producers and importers by the greenhouse gases their products emit, starting at $15 per ton and rising each year, with the rate doubling to $30 in any year after emissions miss the schedule. About 70% of the money would go back to households as a monthly cash payment, with the amount phasing out for people making over $80,000 ($130,000 for couples). The rest would fund roads, transit, water systems, clean-energy research, and aid for workers and communities that depend on fossil fuel jobs.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and middle-income households, who would receive a monthly cash rebate larger than the higher energy prices most of them would face. Also workers in fossil-fuel-dependent industries, who would get wage insurance, retraining, and pension help, and communities getting infrastructure money with a requirement that projects use American-made materials and pay local prevailing wages.

how_it_helps.text: The bill rebates 70% of net carbon fee revenue as a monthly dividend to every eligible adult (half a share per child), and the dividend does not count as income for any federal or state benefits program.
The dividend phases out only above $80,000 of income for individuals and $130,000 for joint filers, so lower-income households keep the full payment.

5% of net revenue funds a worker transition program modeled on trade adjustment assistance, including wage insurance, relocation, early retirement, and pension and health benefits for workers displaced by the fees.

20% of net revenue goes to infrastructure, including highways, transit, rail, airports, drinking water, rural broadband, and the Superfund, with Buy American requirements and Davis-Bacon prevailing wages attached.

A carbon border fee on imported fuels and carbon-intensive goods such as steel, cement, and aluminum is meant to keep foreign producers from undercutting US manufacturers that pay the carbon fee, and US exporters get comparable refunds.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers, refiners, and importers pay the fee and pass it into energy and goods prices. Households earning above the phaseout thresholds face higher prices while their rebate shrinks by 5% for each $1,000 over the limit, so they bear a net cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and higher earners

drawbacks.text: The fee is charged upstream but reaches everyone through higher gasoline, heating, and electricity prices; households above the $80,000/$130,000 phaseout thresholds pay those prices while their dividend shrinks, leaving them with a net loss.
The fee rate climbs $15 per ton every year, and doubles to $30 per year after any year in which emissions miss the reduction target, so prices could rise steeply if the schedule is not met.
Unlike many benefit programs, the carbon dividend is counted in gross income and taxed, slightly reducing its value.

Even with the border fee, energy-intensive industries would face new costs during the years the fee ramps up, and critics of carbon pricing generally argue that costs pass through faster than any rebate arrives; the bill addresses this with an advance dividend paid the month before the first fee collection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design deliberately shifts the burden away from ordinary households: most of the money goes straight back as a monthly payment that phases out only for higher earners, and 5% is reserved for the workers and communities the fee would hurt most. The real risk is price shock from a fast-rising fee, though the border adjustment and export refunds are meant to protect industrial competitiveness. The main honest objection is distributional: the roughly 30% of revenue spent on infrastructure and research means households above the phaseout pay in more than they get back, which is how the bill funds its goals.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the two-year Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Coons of Delaware introduced the bill with Senator Dianne Feinstein of California on July 25, 2019.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the day it was introduced; that was the last action it ever received.
The bill never received a hearing, markup, floor vote, or roll-call vote of any kind before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and their customers avoided the carbon fee entirely, since the status quo remained in place. No ordinary household ever received the dividend the bill promised, because the bill was never advanced by the committee that controlled it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers, thanks to inaction

for.name: Sen. Chris Coons
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Climate Action Rebate Act in the Senate on July 25, 2019.

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, the Senate's only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup and never reported the bill out after its July 2019 referral; the bill's action history ends there.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chairman, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both Senate supporters were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; no roll call was ever taken, and the bill's committee of referral had a Republican chairman in the 116th Congress.

industries.industry: Oil, gas, and coal producers, refiners, and importers
industries.note: They would pay the carbon fee on every ton of emissions from their fuels and pass it into consumer prices. Blocking the bill preserved the fossil fuel industry's cost-free use of the atmosphere; the same delay cost ordinary households the monthly rebate the fee would have funded.

industries.industry: Carbon capture and direct air capture companies
industries.note: The bill pays facilities the going carbon fee rate for every ton of carbon dioxide captured and stored, funded from the same fee revenue.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and clean technology firms
industries.note: A rising carbon fee makes their products relatively cheaper, and 5% of revenue funds Energy Department research and commercialization in storage, grid modernization, and electric vehicles.
Domestic plants pay the fee through fuel costs but gain a border fee on competing imports and Buy American rules on all funded projects; importers of carbon-intensive goods pay the border fee.
20% of net revenue flows to highways, transit, rail, airports, and water systems, with prevailing-wage requirements that raise pay on those projects.
